implementation_notes: MRI exposes no atomic primitives to Ruby code, and the GVL means two Ruby threads do not execute bytecode simultaneously - so for MRI the correct answer is a Mutex and there is no reason to want a hardware atomic. JRuby and TruffleRuby do expose java.util.concurrent.atomic through the Java interop layer, and that is where compareAndSet is available. For counting and stats, Concurrent::Map (from concurrent-ruby) or a Mutex around an Integer. Ruby's Integer assignment is not atomic even where the GVL exists, so a counter increment must still be under a lock.
idiom_name: Mutex for MRI; java.util.concurrent.atomic via JRuby interop; concurrent-ruby for shared maps
code_sketch:
# MRI: the GVL means no bytecode race, but Integer assignment is still not
# an indivisible read-modify-write. A Mutex makes it explicit and portable.
@mutex = Mutex.new

def bump!
  @mutex.synchronize { @count += 1 }
end

# JRuby / TruffleRuby: real atomics through the Java interop layer
#   counter = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong.new(0)
#   counter.increment_and_get

require 'concurrent'
counts = Concurrent::Map.new            # concurrent-safe shared map
pitfalls: Integer += is a read-modify-write in Ruby even under the GVL - the GVL guarantees no interleaving of bytecode, not that the operation is indivisible across a context switch.
MRI has no atomic API at all; reaching for java.util.concurrent.atomic makes the code JRuby-only and breaks on MRI at load time.
JRuby and TruffleRuby do not have the GVL, so a piece of code that is safe on MRI can be racy on JRuby - test on both.
A spin loop on MRI blocks every other thread in the process, so 'non-blocking' is strictly worse than a Mutex there.
alternative: A Mutex around the read-modify-write, which is correct on every Ruby implementation; concurrent-ruby's Concurrent::Map for shared key-value state
